title: 0981-goal-based-competitive-balance-index
universal_lens: The competitive balance of a league is formalized as the statistical deviation from an ideal independent-Poisson goal-scoring process. By mapping scorelines to a Skellam distribution, perfect parity emerges as a null hypothesis, rigorously tested via a likelihood-ratio statistic converging to a chi-squared distribution.
gsi_mapping: In GSI, observed match scorelines serve as empirical data points for Bayesian inference over latent team scoring intensities. The Goal-Based Index (GBI) acts as a conformal test statistic, quantifying the posterior probability that the league's underlying generative parameters deviate from the perfectly balanced prior state.
gse_mapping: GSE utilizes the GBI as a situational state-transition metric. A high GBI value signals a regime shift toward oligopolistic dominance, prompting dynamic adjustments in predictive models. It maps the micro-level Poisson outcomes to macro-level structural stability and revenue generation within the sports ecosystem.

primitives.verbatim_quote: ## Equations / math / assumptions - Assumption 1: goals X_ijk ~ independent Poisson(λ_ijk).

primitives.assumptions: Goal events occur independently over continuous time within a fixed match duration.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Violated by extreme weather, tactical parking-the-bus strategies, or red cards causing severe temporal clustering.

primitives.name: Skellam Goal Difference Symmetry
primitives.verbatim_quote: Goal difference Y_ij = X_ij1 - X_ji0 ~ **Skellam(λ,λ)** with pmf **P(Y_ij=k) = e^{-2λ}·I_{|k|}(2λ)**; pairwise symmetry P(S1>S2)=P(S1<S2) extends through tiebreakers (GD, GS, head-to-head).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Y_ij: integer goal difference; λ: symmetric scoring intensity; I_|k|: modified Bessel function of the first kind
primitives.assumptions: Both teams share identical underlying scoring intensities (λ_i = λ_j = λ) under perfect balance.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when home-field advantage introduces asymmetric intensities (λ_home ≠ λ_away).

layer2.mapping: Derives the exact probabilistic kernel for pairwise matchups, enabling GSE to calculate precise upset probabilities without relying on win/draw/loss approximations.
layer2.telemetry: Distribution of goal differences across all league fixtures.

primitives.name: Goal-Based Index Chi-Squared Test
primitives.verbatim_quote: - **Theorem 3:** under perfect balance, **(2N-1)·GBI ~ χ2_{2N-1}** asymptotically (Taylor expansion of the Poisson likelihood-ratio statistic: -2logΛ = 2Σ X_ijk log(X_ijk/λ̂) ≈ (2N-1)·GBI).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: N: number of matches; GBI: dimensionless goodness-of-fit index; χ^2: chi-squared distribution
primitives.assumptions: Large sample size (asymptotic regime) and valid maximum likelihood estimation of the baseline intensity.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity occurs if estimated intensity λ̂ approaches zero, rendering the Taylor expansion invalid.

layer2.telemetry: Computed GBI value and corresponding p-value against the chi-squared distribution.

reasoning_traces.think:
The derivation begins by modeling football matches not as deterministic outcomes but as realizations of independent Poisson processes. Under the null hypothesis of perfect competitive balance, every team possesses an identical underlying scoring intensity, denoted as λ. This assumption elegantly simplifies the complex dynamics of a league into a single-parameter system. Consequently, the goal difference between any two equally matched teams follows a Skellam distribution, which is the difference of two independent Poisson random variables. The probability mass function of this distribution relies heavily on the modified Bessel function of the first kind, ensuring that the probability of Team A beating Team B exactly equals the probability of Team B beating Team A. This mathematical symmetry guarantees that any permutation of the final league standings is equally likely, establishing a robust theoretical foundation for parity. To empirically test this ideal state, the author constructs the Goal-Based Index (GBI). Through a rigorous Taylor expansion of the Poisson likelihood-ratio statistic, it is proven that a scaled version of the GBI asymptotically follows a chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom determined by the number of matches. This transforms the abstract concept of competitive balance into a concrete, statistically testable metric. Unlike traditional indices that rely solely on aggregated points (like the Herfindahl index), the GBI leverages the granular information contained within actual scorelines. Simulation studies confirm its exceptional power, demonstrating that the test can detect even minute deviations—such as a single dominant team among twenty—with a type-I error strictly controlled at 5%. Ultimately, panel regressions reveal that this scoreline-derived index significantly explains variations in league revenues, outperforming standard concentration metrics.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This framework inherits deeply from mid-20th-century stochastic process theory, specifically the application of Poisson distributions to rare events pioneered by R.D. Clarke and later adapted to sports analytics by Dixon and Coles. The use of the Skellam distribution traces back to J.G. Skellam's 1948 work on the difference of Poisson variates. By bridging these classical statistical tools with modern econometric panel regressions, the research elevates competitive balance from a heuristic sociological concept to a rigorous, quantifiable mathematical invariant, echoing the evolution of market efficiency tests in financial economics.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: From a theory of mind perspective, the model treats each football club as an autonomous agent optimizing for point accumulation under a shared, albeit noisy, environmental constraint. The independent Poisson assumption implies that agents operate without explicit collusion, their offensive outputs driven by internal latent capabilities rather than direct manipulation of opponents' defenses beyond standard play. However, the breakdown of the GBI null hypothesis reveals the emergence of strategic asymmetries. When a few agents drastically increase their effective λ through superior resource allocation (e.g., player acquisitions), they disrupt the equilibrium. The resulting skew in the Skellam distributions reflects a shift from a cooperative, parity-seeking ecosystem to a competitive, dominance-driven hierarchy, fundamentally altering the incentive structures for all participating entities.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: A critical cross-layer veto must be applied regarding the independence assumption inherent in the Poisson model. In reality, goal scoring events are often temporally clustered; a goal scored changes the tactical posture of both teams, dynamically altering subsequent λ values within the same match. Furthermore, the bivariate nature of match outcomes means home-team and away-team scores are rarely perfectly independent. If these dependencies are strong, the variance of the goal difference may exceed the mean, leading to overdispersion that artificially inflates the GBI. Therefore, before deploying the GBI as a definitive revenue predictor in GSE, one must verify that the residuals do not exhibit significant autocorrelation or require a more complex copula structure, such as the Dixon-Coles adjustment, to prevent spurious statistical significance.
